planting.note: Start seed indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant out while nights are still cool; this 2024 AAS Regional Winner also suits a late-summer sowing for a fall crop in most regions.

directions: Skytree grows noticeably taller and more upright than typical broccoli, carrying its 4- to 8-inch central crown well above the foliage on a sturdy stalk that stays easy to harvest without bending or kneeling. The compact 10- to 12-inch footprint lets it fit into containers and tight raised beds despite its height, and judges noted the tender, sweet-flavored florets and stems held up well under heat stress. Keep soil evenly moist and feed at transplanting for the fastest, most uniform crown development, and harvest the central head promptly to encourage a flush of side shoots afterward.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once nights stay reliably warm; this 2023 AAS National Winner is an indeterminate plum type that needs staking or caging for its full season.

directions: Zenzei is a vigorous indeterminate Roma-type plum tomato bred for canning and freezing, setting heavy clusters of 4- to 5-inch, 3- to 8-ounce oblong fruits with dense, meaty flesh and little internal cavity. Its naturally tidy growth habit resists sprawl better than many indeterminate plum types, and judges praised its early, high yield along with resistance to blossom end rot and leaf spotting. Stake or cage plants at transplanting since the heavy fruit clusters need support, and keep watering consistent through fruit set to avoid cracking; no pruning is required to keep the plant productive.

common_name: Red Plume Gaillardia (AAS-Winning Double Brick-Red Blanket Flower)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6 weeks before the last frost or direct sow once soil has warmed; this 1991 AAS Flower Winner behaves as a tender perennial in zones 7-11 and is typically grown as a warm-season annual bedding plant farther north.

directions: Red Plume forms a dwarf, dense mound topped with fully double, brick-red blooms 1.5 to 2 inches across, a striking break from the single daisy-form flowers typical of blanket flower. Flowers are held on sturdy stems well above the foliage, making the plant useful as a mid-height filler for background color without staking. Plant in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; it tolerates heat and drought readily but declines quickly in soggy or heavy clay ground. It performs well in containers and hanging baskets, and deadheading spent blooms keeps the display going through the warm season.

common_name: Connecticut Yankee Delphinium (AAS-Winning Bushy Branching Delphinium)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8 to 10 weeks before the last frost with a period of cold stratification to improve germination, then transplant out after frost danger passes; this 1963 AAS National Winner flowers the first year from an early start and returns reliably as a perennial in cooler climates.

directions: Connecticut Yankee broke from the tall, single-spike delphinium tradition with a bushy, heavily branched habit that produces many 2.5-inch flowers in blue, lavender, purple, and white all on the same compact plant, and it rarely needs staking the way taller delphinium types do. Grow in rich, well-drained soil in full sun with some afternoon shade in hot climates, since delphinium resents both waterlogged soil and prolonged summer heat. It performs best as a true perennial in cooler zones; in warmer regions treat it as a short-lived perennial or cool-season annual. Cut spent flower stalks back after the first bloom flush to encourage a second, lighter round of flowering later in the season.

common_name: Cheer Blue Delphinium (AAS-Winning Compact Seed Delphinium)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8 to 10 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once hard frost danger has passed; this 2020 AAS National Winner flowers earlier and longer into summer than older delphinium types and is typically grown as a cool-season bedding annual.

directions: Cheer Blue stays compact at just 10 to 12 inches tall, far shorter than classic border delphinium, while still delivering the same intense blue color on an unusually uniform, well-branched plant covered in 1-inch flowers. Judges valued how early it comes into bloom and how long it holds color before fading in summer heat, making it a good choice for bedding displays, mixed containers, and small landscape beds. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil and keep moisture consistent, since this small-rooted selection dries out faster than larger delphinium types. It needs no staking and performs best where summers are mild to moderately warm.
